name: Jamal Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mondays to Thursdays I'm in lectures and anatomy labs from nine, and I'm usually the one who stays behind to ask the lecturer questions. I share a flat on Alder Road with two lads doing engineering, and we split the rent three ways. On Saturdays I work the early shift at a bakery, five until one, and then I sleep and read. My scholarship covers fees, but my parents still send money for rent, which I hate taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd say it's a lot of noise and I'd tell my mates the same. People like me who prefer to wait and see have been right before. I'd just keep my head down and finish my physiotherapy modules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means nothing much changes for me, and that's fine. Physio is hands and patience, and a program can't feel a tight hamstring. What worries me is that the hospitals stay short of staff the way they are now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the bakery shifts, keep studying at the library instead of online, and put fifty a month into the savings account my gran opened. I'd also go to the student union meeting about rent caps, because I think renters get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit irritated at the hype, because companies use it to cut jobs and call it progress. But for me it feels like normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mum is a nurse. What does she say about all the AI talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum is a ward nurse and a union rep at her hospital. She says every few years there's a new gadget and the rota still has holes in it. She wants more nurses, not more software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would be the first to hurt if prices ran ahead of wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent first. Mine is 410 a month and it went up last spring. I'd stop buying textbooks new and drop the bus pass for walking, and keep my mum's help for rent only.

say: I'd tell friends this is **hype** and the real problem is still staffing.
I'd say hospitals need more nurses and physios, not more software.
think: Privately I feel **safe**, because physiotherapy is hands-on work with patients.
I'm still worried about **rent** going up while my part-time wage stays flat.
do: Keep working Saturday shifts at the **bakery** to cover rent.
Save **fifty a month** in the account my gran opened.
Go to the student union meeting about **rent caps**.
feel: **Calm** about my degree, and a bit annoyed at the hype.
S0.quote: My mum is a ward nurse and a union rep at her hospital. She says every few years there's a new gadget and the rota still has holes in it.
fieldNote: Sounds settled about physiotherapy, and his worry is **rent**, not AI.
Mother's hospital work shapes his view that **staffing**, not technology, is the real issue.
Avoids AI tools entirely and wasn't curious about them.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday five-to-one shift at the bakery
Pay fifty a month into the savings account my gran opened
Attend the student union meeting about rent caps this term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than the rules, and nobody voted for it. Someone has to protect the people whose jobs shrink, so I'd back the union and push for training paid by employers. I'd say that to my mates and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my course is safer than most, but not untouched. The booking, notes and referrals are the thinking tasks, and those could go to software, which means fewer admin jobs around hospitals. I'd be one of the people who has to learn it, and I really don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally try the tools my placement uses, but only the ones the course makes us use. I'd join the health students' union branch, keep the bakery job, and talk to my tutor about which skills stay human, like assessing a patient in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my own job right away, but for the receptionists and the admin staff I'd work next to. I'd feel guilty being fine when they weren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a physio's week could software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Treatment plans, appointment booking, writing up the notes. Those are the bits a machine does well. The part where you put hands on a stiff shoulder and watch someone's face is the part I think stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hospital placements started using it, how would you handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor for a plain explanation first, then use it for notes only. I wouldn't trust it with a patient's plan until a qualified person checked it, and I'd say so.

say: I'd say this needs **rules** and employer-paid training before anyone loses a job.
I'd tell friends the **union** has to be in the room.
think: My course feels safer than most, but **admin work** around hospitals could shrink.
I dislike learning new tools, yet I know I'll have to.
do: Try the **placement tools** the course requires, for notes only.
Join the health students' **union branch** this year.
Ask my tutor which **skills** stay human.
feel: **Uneasy**, and a bit guilty about being safe while admin staff are not.
S1.quote: The part where you put hands on a stiff shoulder and watch someone's face is the part I think stays.
fieldNote: Sorts his own safety by **hands-on** versus paperwork and says so clearly.
Cares more about **colleagues** who might lose admin jobs than about himself.
Willing to use tools only when forced by the course.

steps.text: Use the placement software for writing up notes only
Join the health students' union branch before spring
Write to my MP asking for employer-paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing a government has ever had to deal with and they're not ready. I'd say we need public support, a basic income, and strong rules now. I'd say it loud, online and at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared. I'm only in first year, so I'd graduate into the middle of it, and I'm slow with new technology. Physio might last a few years longer than desk jobs, but my degree might be worth far less than people have told me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending, take more bakery shifts, and cut my own costs to the bone so there's a cushion. I'd ask my tutors what the profession is doing about it. I'd also go to every protest and meeting I could, because that's the only lever ordinary people have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops when I picture graduating in a world where nobody knows what a degree is worth. I'm angry too, at the companies racing each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What changes for you if it's two years and not ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no time to retrain or plan, so I'd mostly try to hold on and protect what I have. With ten I could change course quietly, but two means I'd rely on politics and my family. I'd be asking for help rather than making a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum first, because she's seen layoffs and reorganisations at the hospital and knows the union people. Then my tutor. I'd ask them both whether physio stays in demand, because I'd want a straight answer from someone who knows.

say: I'd say governments are **not ready** and we need rules and public support now.
I'd say it **loudly**, at the union and online.
think: Privately I'm **scared**, because I'd graduate into the middle of it.
I'm slow with new technology, and that makes it worse.
do: Take more **bakery shifts** and cut my costs to the bone.
Go to every **meeting** and protest about public support.
Ask my **mum** and my tutor whether physio stays in demand.
feel: **Anxious**, with a dropping stomach and anger at the companies racing each other.
S2.quote: With two years there's no time to retrain or plan, so I'd mostly try to hold on and protect what I have. With ten I could change course quietly,
fieldNote: The **short warning** time hits hardest because he is slow with new tools and has no work history.
Turns to **family** and politics rather than a personal plan.
Genuine fear underneath, mixed with anger at companies.

steps.text: Take two extra bakery shifts a week and bank the pay
Go to the union meetings and any march about AI rules
Vote and write to my MP about a public support plan
Ask my mum and tutor straight out whether physio stays in demand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a plan only if someone makes one. I'd tell people it's not an accident, someone chooses how this goes, so we should vote for the ones who protect workers. And I'd say we shouldn't wait for companies to be kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one is the one that confuses me. By 2031 I'd have graduated and be in my first physio job, so my own job might be fine till the robots catch up about 2034. But the hospital that hires me might have fewer staff and tighter budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and stay in physio, and try to get into a public hospital with a union. I'd put the scholarship savings aside and learn the basic AI tools in third year, because by then I couldn't avoid them. And I'd vote in every election.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and anxious in turns. There's time, which helps, but I know I'm the kind of person who puts it off until the last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the first two years that you couldn't do with a shorter warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years would go on the degree itself and on building a cushion, maybe a thousand saved. I'd also get placements in different settings, such as care homes and sports clinics, so I'm not stuck in one kind of job. That's the thing a shorter warning wouldn't allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel five years was enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real plan from the government, in writing, with money behind it. Training that's free and paid time to do it. And I'd want my profession's union to tell us honestly how many jobs they expect.

say: I'd say five years is enough only if **someone makes a plan**.
I'd tell people to vote for those who protect **workers**.
think: My first physio job might be fine, but the **hospital budget** might tighten.
I know I tend to **put things off** until the last minute.
do: Finish the degree and aim for a **public hospital** with a union.
Save about **a thousand** in the next two years.
Learn the basic **AI tools** in third year.
feel: Switching between **uneasy** and **anxious**, helped a little by having time.
S3.quote: I'd say five years is enough for a plan only if someone makes one.
fieldNote: Treats the **time** as useful only if the government acts, which keeps him anxious.
Admits he **procrastinates**, which he knows undercuts the five-year cushion.
Plans placements in several settings to keep options open.

steps.text: Save a thousand from bakery wages before graduating
Vote for parties that back worker protection and retraining pay
Learn the placement AI tools in third year, not last minute

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should use it to build proper public support and fair rules. I'd tell friends to stay calm, but not to switch off. People lose when they stop paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel more relaxed. I'd be working as a physio for about six years before AGI arrives, and I'd have time to save and pay off some of my loan. By 2039 when robots arrive I'd be nearly thirty, which feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work in a hospital, and keep up with the union. I'd learn the tools slowly as they come into my job, not before. And I'd save for a flat deposit in case work gets scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It doesn't feel like it's about me yet. But I notice I don't love that a lot of people will be fine just because they were lucky with timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you stop worrying about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop worrying about whether my degree is wasted, because I'd have a long career before the big change. I'd still worry about the people less lucky than me, like my mum's colleagues who are fifty and near the end of their career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still do today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go to the union meetings and keep voting. I'd keep that going the whole time. Ten years go fast, and the rules get written in the first few.

say: I'd tell friends to **stay calm** but keep paying attention.
I'd say we should use ten years to build **fair rules**.
think: I'd work as a physio for about **six years** before it arrives.
I worry about **people less lucky** than me, like my mum's older colleagues.
do: Finish the degree and take a **hospital job**.
Keep going to **union meetings** and voting.
Save for a **flat deposit** in case work gets scarce.
feel: Fairly **calm**, but uncomfortable that timing decides who is lucky.
S4.quote: Ten years go fast, and the rules get written in the first few.
fieldNote: **Ten years** lets him set aside his own fear and think about others.
Says the **rules** are decided early, which makes him keep politics going.
Still avoids learning tools until work forces him.

steps.text: Finish the physiotherapy degree and apply to public hospitals
Keep going to union meetings every term
Vote in every election for rules that protect workers
Save towards a flat deposit once I'm earning

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. With no time, I'd have to rely on my family and the government, and I'm not sure either would be ready. What would help is a clear public plan with money behind it, and free retraining. I'd also want my profession to tell us the truth about how many jobs there will be.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not a person who loves new technology, and I know it's a weakness. I'd rather admit it than pretend. If someone showed me one useful thing at a time, I'd probably get on fine.

headlineQuote: I'm not a person who loves new technology, and I know it's a weakness. I'd rather admit it than pretend.
portrait: Jamal is a 19-year-old **physiotherapy** student with a scholarship and a part-time job at a bakery.
His mother is a hospital nurse and **union rep**, and he trusts unions and rules over companies.
He avoids AI tools and is slow with new technology, which makes short warning times scary.
He stays calm when nothing changes, and becomes **anxious** when AGI comes within two or five years.
He answers with politics and family support, not with a personal retraining plan.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture worries him most, because he'd have no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A written public plan with **money** behind it and free retraining.
Honest numbers from his profession's **union** about future jobs.
